rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports that appear to make Quranic arrangement a matter of independent judgment are unreliable and contradicted by abundant evidence.
rows.anchor: وما يدل بظاهره من الآثار على أنه إجتهادي معارض ساقط عن درجة الإعتبار

rows.speaker: عبدالله بن الزبير عن أبيه
rows.claim: Al-Harith brought the final two Bara'a verses; al-Zubayr and Umar testified the Prophet had recited them, and Umar said three verses would have formed a separate sura.
rows.anchor: بسنده عن عبدالله بن الزبير عن أبيه قال أتى الحرث بن خزيمة بهاتين الآيتين

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy said that after the compilers mistook 9:127 for the final revelation, the Prophet recited him the last two verses of Bara'a.
rows.anchor: فقال أبي أن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم أقرأني بعد هذا آيتين

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority hold that the arrangement of suras is divinely prescribed rather than the result of independent judgment.
rows.anchor: في كونه إجتهاديا أو توقيفيا خلاف والجمهور على الثاني

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الأنباري
rows.claim: Al-Anbari says the Quran was sent down as a whole to the lowest heaven and then revealed piecemeal; Gabriel specified each verse's and sura's position, so rearranging it corrupts its order.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الأنباري أنزل الله تعالى القرآن كله إلى سماء الدنيا ثم فرقه

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani says the sura order matches the Preserved Tablet and that the Prophet reviewed the accumulated Quran with Gabriel annually, twice in his final year.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني بترتيب السور هكذا هو عند الله تعالى في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi shares al-Kirmani's account, which al-Alusi says is also transmitted from a large group.
rows.anchor: وقال الطيبي مثله وهو المروي عن جمع غفير إلا أنه يشكل على هذا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas asked Uthman why al-Anfal and Bara'a were paired without a basmala and placed among the seven long suras; Uthman explained that he presumed they belonged together because their stories resembled each other and the Prophet had not clarified.
rows.anchor: عن إبن عباس قال قلت لعثمان ما حملكم على أن عمدتم إلى الأنفال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uthman's explanation indicates that independent judgment entered the arrangement of al-Anfal and Bara'a; al-Bayhaqi therefore exempts these two from his otherwise fully prescribed order.
rows.anchor: فهذا يدل على أن الإجتهاد دخل في ترتيب السور ولهذا ذهب البيهقي

rows.speaker: البيهقي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqi holds that every sura's order is prescribed except for al-Anfal and Bara'a; al-Suyuti found this answer appealing when he could not resolve the question.
rows.anchor: ذهب البيهقي إلى أن جميع السور ترتيبها توقيفي إلا براءة والأنفال

rows.speaker: الإمام السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti's relief at al-Bayhaqi's answer came after he had found himself unable to resolve the issue.
rows.anchor: انشرح صدر الإمام السيوطي لما ضاق ذرعا عن الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers that the present codex matches the Quran's order in the Preserved Tablet: the Prophet must have specified or signaled the positions, and the Companions' eventual consensus shows they had certain knowledge.
rows.anchor: والذي ينشرح له صدر هذا الفقير هو ما أنشرحت له صدور الجمع الغفير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uthman may have acted on a presumption about Bara'a and al-Anfal, while others recognized a textual indication and accepted his arrangement; Umar's inspired judgments offer a parallel.
rows.anchor: وعثمان رضي الله تعالى عنه وإن لم يقف على ما يفيده القطع في براءة والأنفال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ibn Abbas exchange does not conclusively prove independent arrangement: the question could seek the reason for not separating the suras, and Uthman could be stating his own initial rationale.
rows.anchor: والسؤال منه وجوابه ليسا قطعيين في الدلالة على الإستقلال لجواز أن يكون السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given the community's consensus on this codex, isolated reports and unusual narrations should not overturn its established order.
rows.anchor: بعد إجماع الأمة على هذا المصحف لا ينبغي أن يصاخ إلى آحاد الأخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech has five compositional ranks: letters form words, words form useful sentences, sentences are arranged into prose, prose may be rhymed, and metrical speech becomes poetry when meter is intended.
rows.anchor: ضم الحروف المبسوطة بعضها إلى بعض فتحصل الكلمات الثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran gathers the beauties of all speech forms in an unsurpassed order, free of flaws and with qualities unmatched by other styles.
rows.anchor: والقرآن جامع لمحاسن الجميع بنظم مكتس أبهى حلل ومتعر عن كل خلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is rightly called speech but cannot be classified as a letter, sermon, or sajʿ; a discerning listener immediately distinguishes it from other compositions.
rows.anchor: لا يصح أن يقال له رسالة أو خطابة أو سجع كما يصح أن يقال هو كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even al-Walid could recognize that the Quran's composition differs from ordinary literary forms.
rows.anchor: وهذا مما لا خفاء فيه على الرجال حتى على الوليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic eloquence draws the best from forceful, elevated speech, clear easy speech, and fluent flowing speech, producing grandeur and sweetness together despite their usual tension.
rows.anchor: حازت بلاغة القرآن من كل قسم من هذه الأقسام أو فرصة وأخذت من كل نوع أعظم شعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's reports about past peoples, earlier communities, and former laws were numerous and exact, although only exceptional scriptural scholars would know them after a lifetime of study.
rows.anchor: تضمن ما يحكم العرف بكثرته من أخبار القرون الماضية والأمم البادية والشرائع الدائرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran's detailed past reports are miraculous because they came through Muhammad, an unlettered man who neither read nor wrote.
rows.anchor: مما كان لا يعلم منه القصة الواحدة إلا الفذ من أحبار أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also demonstrates miraculous knowledge of what many people concealed in their minds, without their revealing it in speech or action.
rows.anchor: مع الأعلام بما في ضمائر كثيرين من غير أن يظهر ذلك منهم بقول أو فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third objection to the ṣarfah theory is that it entails the Quran's like having been ordinary before the alleged removal of people's ability, so prior Arabic speech could have matched it.
rows.anchor: أنه يستلزم أن يكون مثل القرآن معتادا من قبل لتحقق الصرفة من بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Murtada's specific argument is that if incapacity came from loss of knowledge, people would have announced this extraordinary event and it would have become widely known; their silence refutes it.
rows.anchor: وهو خاص بمذهب المرتضى أنه لو كان الإعجاز بفقدهم العلوم لتناطقوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge in 17:88 shows the Arabs remained capable yet could not match the Quran; removing their power would make the challenge pointless, like challenging the dead. This supplements rather than replaces the other evidence.
rows.anchor: فإنه يدل على عجزهم مع بقاء قدرهم ولو سلبوا القدرة لم تبق فائدة

rows.speaker: الآمدي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Amidi and others locate the Quran's miracle in its entirety, especially the combined force of its order, eloquence, and reports of the unseen; al-Alusi says many accepted this view.
rows.anchor: وقال الآمدي وغيره الإعجاز بجملته وبالنظر إلى نظمه وبلاغته وإخباره عن الغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accidental meter does not make speech poetry: poetry requires intentional meter, and even ordinary speech can happen to scan.
rows.anchor: الشعر ما قصد وزنه وحيث لا قصد لا شعر وقد يعرض للبلغاء في سرد خطبهم

rows.speaker: الوليد
rows.claim: After hearing the Prophet recite, al-Walid told Abu Jahl that the Quran resembled no poetry or jinn verse he knew and praised its sweetness, beauty, fruitfulness, and overpowering force.
rows.anchor: قال الوليد لما قرأ عليه النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم القرآن فكأنما رق له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First, the challenge addressed the eloquent masters; ordinary people's inability proves nothing because they lacked the relevant craft, while the elite's failure establishes the miracle.
rows.anchor: فلأن التفاوت بين لمن تحدى به من البلغاء ولذا لم يعارض وغيرهم عم عن ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Second, the ability to produce one or two eloquent phrases or verses does not imply the ability to compose a full sermon or poem.
rows.anchor: القدرة على البعض لا تستلزم القدرة على الكل ولهذا نجد الكثير قادرا على بليغ فقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Third, the Companions disputed whether particular revealed material counted as Quran, not whether its eloquence was miraculous, so that dispute is irrelevant here.
rows.anchor: أن الصحابة لم يختلفوا فيما أختلفوا فيه أنه نازل على النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fourth, a demand for proof can be explained by the earlier rationale, by questions about composition and order, or by extra caution over a grave matter.
rows.anchor: فلأن طلب البينة لما قدمناه في الفائدة السادسة أو للوضع والترتيب كما قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fifth, miracles appear in the field at which each age excels; an audience otherwise might suppose its own masters could match the prophet if fully trained.
rows.anchor: فلأن المعجز يظهر في كل زمان من جنس ما يغلب ويبلغ فيه الغاية القصوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic eloquence was the Arabs' foremost distinction, and they displayed their challenge by hanging the seven celebrated odes at the Kaaba; the Prophet's unmatched Quran therefore proved divine origin.
rows.anchor: والبلاغة قد بلغت في ذلك العهد حدها وكان فيها فخارهم حتى علقت السبع بباب الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated, accurate Quranic reports about unseen events are extraordinary by ordinary standards; that unusual success is itself the relevant sense of a miracle.
rows.anchor: فإن الإخبار عن الغائبات مع التكرر والإصابة غير معتاد ولا معنى لكونه معجزا غير هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although one or two correct predictions need not be supernatural, repeated successes can be; the Quran contains enough unseen reports to exceed customary chance.
rows.anchor: لا يلزم من عدم كون الإصابة في المرة والمرتين من الخوارق أن لا تكون الإصابة في الكرات الكثيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Astrologers' false predictions have no evidentiary force, while accurate eclipse predictions come from their ordinary calculations; Quranic reports of the unseen are unlike these.
rows.anchor: ما كان كاذبا منها لا إحتجاج وما كان صادقا وتكررت الإصابة فيه كالكسوف والخسوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection from soothsayers is answered as the parallel objection from sorcery is answered.
rows.anchor: وأما أخبار الكهنة فالقول فيها كما في السحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Torah's unseen reports were abundant, extraordinary, and challenged, they too would be miracles and signs of the truth of the one who brought them; this concession does no harm.
rows.anchor: فلأن ما في التوراة من الأخبار بالغيب إن كان كثيرا خارقا للعادة ووقع التحدي به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection does not affect a combined account of the Quran's miracle; if unseen reports alone are proposed, the Quran is miraculous as a whole even if passages without such reports are not individually miraculous.
rows.anchor: فلأنه لا يرد على من يقول وجه الإعجاز مجموع ما تقدم أصلا ومن يقول وجهه مجرد الأخبار بالغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial that the Prophet was taught poetry (36:69) answers the supposed poetic contradiction; the alleged differences in 4:82 concern either defective eloquence or conflicting accounts of the past, neither of which occurs in the Quran.
rows.anchor: لأن المراد به أحد أمرين الأول الإختلاف المناقض للبلاغة والثاني الإختلاف فيما أخبر عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some alleged contradictions are not Quran because they lack mass transmission; other differences of wording reflect different circumstances while describing one underlying reality, such as Adam's origin from earth.
rows.anchor: على أن أمثال بعض ما ذكر من الإختلاف ليس بقرآن لأنه لم يتواتر وأمثال البعض الآخر إختلاف مقال لإختلاف الأحوال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reconciles verses that deny and affirm questioning by placing the denial before the second trumpet and the affirmation afterward.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس حين سأله رجل عن آيات من هذا القبيل بأن نفي المسألة قبل النفخة الثانية

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says questioning is denied while people are occupied with swooning, judgment, and crossing the bridge, but affirmed at other times.
rows.anchor: والسدي بأن نفي المسألة عند تشاغلهم بالصعق والمحاسبة والجواز على الصراط

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud distinguishes the negated asking as people seeking pardon from one another, while the affirmed questioning retains its apparent sense.
rows.anchor: وابن مسعود بأن المسألة المنفية طلب بعضهم العفو من بعض والمثبتة على ظاهر معناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first of the two 'what prevented people from believing' passages refers to God's will that earlier peoples' punishment befall them or that they see punishment in the hereafter; divine will is the true cause, so this is no contradiction.
rows.anchor: إرادة الله تعالى مانعة من وقوع ما ينافي المراد فهذا حصر في السبب الحقيقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second passage refers to people's ordinary astonishment at a human messenger, not a true impediment; that customary obstacle can coexist with faith and does not contradict the first passage.
rows.anchor: إلا إستغراب بعثة البشر رسولا وهو مدلول القول إلتزاما والدال لا يناسب المانعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated wording or meaning always serves a purpose, including breadth of expression, display of eloquence, and added emphasis or intensification.
rows.anchor: وأما التكرار اللفظي والمعنوي فلا يخلو عن فائدة لا تحصل من غير تكرار كبيان إتساع العبارة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Twenty-one Companions transmitted that the Quran was revealed in seven ahruf, and Abu Ubayda explicitly judged the report mass-transmitted.
rows.anchor: روى أحد وعشرون صحابيا حديث نزول القرآن على سبعة أحرف حتى نص أبو عبيدة على تواتره

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: On the pulpit Uthman asked witnesses to testify that the Prophet said the Quran was revealed in seven ahruf, all sound and sufficient; many stood and Uthman joined their testimony.
rows.anchor: أن عثمان رضي الله عنه قال على المنبر أذكر الله رجلا سمع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view treats the seven ahruf report as an obscure expression whose meaning cannot be known; al-Alusi replies that the word's ambiguity alone does not make the report obscure.
rows.anchor: أنه من المشكل الذي لا يدري لإشتراك الحرف وفيه أن مجرد الإشتراك لا يستدعي ذلك

rows.speaker: عياض
rows.claim: Qadi Iyad takes seven as a conventional number for abundance, as Arabs also use seventy and seven hundred for large quantities.
rows.anchor: أن المراد التكثير لا حقيقة العدد وقد جروا على تكثير الآحاد بالسبعة

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from Ubayy says Gabriel first asked the Prophet to recite on one harf, while Michael urged him to request more until the count reached seven.
rows.anchor: حديث أبي كما رواه النسائي أن جبريل وميكائيل أتياني فقعد جبريل عن يميني

rows.speaker: أبي بكرة
rows.claim: In Abu Bakra's report, the Prophet knew the requested allowance had reached its limit when he looked to Michael and Michael fell silent.
rows.anchor: حديث أبي بكرة الذي في آخره فنظرت إلى ميكائيل فسكت فعلمت أنه قد إنتهت العدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports indicate an exact limit of seven, not a loose expression for abundance; the wording in a paucity plural also suggests a limited number.
rows.anchor: أقوى دليل على إرادة الإنحصار بل في جمع القلة نوع إشارة إلى عدم الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view identifies the seven ahruf with the seven canonical readings, but words with seven variants are rare and some words are read in more than seven ways.
rows.anchor: إن المراد بها سبع قرآت وفيه أن ذلك لا يوجد في كلمة واحدة إلا نادر

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti calls it gross ignorance to suppose that the seven ahruf mean the seven readings.
rows.anchor: قال السيوطي قد ظن كثير من القوم أن المراد بها القرآت السبعة وهو جهل قبيح

rows.speaker: إبن عيينة
rows.claim: Ibn Uyayna and others hold that the seven ahruf are seven synonymous expressions for a shared meaning, such as aqbil, taʿal, hallum, ʿajjil, and asriʿ.
rows.anchor: وإليه ذهب إبن عيينة وجمع وأيد برواية حتى بلغ سبعة أحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A supporting report says all seven forms are healing and sufficient, but forbids ending a verse of punishment with mercy or mercy with punishment.
rows.anchor: ما لم تختم آية عذاب برحمة أو رحمة بعذاب

rows.speaker: إبن مسعود
rows.claim: When a man could not pronounce 'al-athim,' Ibn Masud told him to say 'al-fajir' instead.
rows.anchor: أن إبن مسعود أقرأ رجلا ( إن شجرة الزقوم طعام الأثيم ) فقال الرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi treats synonym substitution as a temporary concession for illiterate people struggling with a fixed wording; it was later abrogated, since otherwise recitation by meaning would erase exact-word worship and many subtleties and rulings.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك كان رخصة لعسر تلاوته بلفظ واحد على الأميين ثم نسخ وإلا لجازت روايته بالمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth view says the ahruf are pronunciation modes such as assimilation, clarity, emphatic or light articulation, lengthening, shortening, and stress.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بها كيفية النطق بالتلاوة من إدغام وإظهار وتفخيم وترقيق وإشباع ومد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pronunciation modes do not vary the word or meaning; the word remains one, so this view offers no substantial benefit.
rows.anchor: أن ذلك ليس من الإختلاف الذي يتنوع فيه اللفظ والمعنى واللفظ الواحد بهذه الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sixth view, held by many, identifies the seven ahruf as seven categories; the segment begins listing those categories but does not name them here.
rows.anchor: أن المراد سبعة أصناف وعليه كثيرون ثم أختلفوا في تعيينها فقيل

rows.speaker: إبن خلكان
rows.claim: Ibn Khallikan records that after Saladin captured Aleppo, judge Muhyi al-Din recited a poem predicting Jerusalem's conquest in Rajab, following the Aleppo victory in Safar.
rows.anchor: ذكر إبن خلكان في تاريخه أن السلطان صلاح الدين لما فتح مدينة حلب أنشد القاضي محيي الدين

rows.speaker: القاضي محيي الدين
rows.claim: Asked how he made the prediction, Muhyi al-Din said he derived it from Ibn Barjan's tafsir of 30:2–4; the historian later found that commentary and its calculation.
rows.anchor: فسئل القاضي من أين لك هذا فقال أخذته من تفسير إبن برجان

rows.speaker: إبن الكمال
rows.claim: A well-known example is Ibn al-Kamal's inference that Sultan Selim would conquer Egypt from 21:105.
rows.anchor: ومن المشهور إستنباط إبن الكمال فتح مصر على يد السلطان سليم من قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi urges fairness toward Sufi masters in the Muhammadan spiritual circle and suspicion of one's own limited understanding when obstacles prevent access to their insights; he compares this to trusting those who saw the crescent.
rows.anchor: فالأنصاف كل الإنصاف التسليم للسادة الصوفية الذين هم مركز للدائرة المحمدية

rows.speaker: شيدلة
rows.claim: Shidla counts fifty-five names for the Quran, and al-Suyuti discusses the reasons for these names in al-Itqan.
rows.anchor: أن لكتاب الله تعالى أسماء أنهاها شيدلة في البرهان إلى خمسة وخمسين أسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the many Quranic names ultimately reduce to Quran and Furqan, just as the divine names return to the attributes of beauty and majesty.
rows.anchor: وعندي أنها كلها ترجع بعد التأمل الصادق إلى القرآن والفرقان رجوع أسماء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i and a group hold that Quran is a proper, non-derived name specific to the revelation to Muhammad, unhamzated and treated as a definite name.
rows.anchor: المروي عن الشافعي وبه قال جماعة أنه اسم علم غير مشتق خاص بهذا الكلام المنزل

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Ashari and others derive Quran from qarantu, 'I joined,' because its suras, verses, and letters are joined together; on this view it has no hamza and its n is original.
rows.anchor: والمنقول عن الأشعري وأقوام أنه مشتق من قرنت الشيء إذا ضممته إليه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra derives Quran from qara'in, 'indications,' because its verses confirm and resemble one another; this derivation also has no hamza and treats n as original.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء هو مشتق من القرائن لأن الآيات فيه يصدق بعضها بعضا ويشبه بعضها بعضا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj rejects the unhamzated derivations and treats the hamza as original, explaining its omission as lightening with the vowel transferred to the preceding letter; he derives the word from qarʾ, gathering.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج هذا القول غلط والصواب أن ترك الهمزة فيه من باب التخفيف ونقل حركتها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda explains the name as referring to the gathering of the suras.
rows.anchor: وسمى به لأنه جمع السور كما قال أبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains Quran as a gathering of the fruits of earlier scriptures.
rows.anchor: أو ثمرات الكتب السالفة كما قال الراغب

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub connects Quran to the reciter bringing it out from his mouth, using the expression that a she-camel has never brought forth a fetal membrane.
rows.anchor: لأن القاريء يظهره من فيه أخذا من قولهم ما قرأت الناقة سلى قط كما حكى عن قطرب

rows.speaker: اللحياني
rows.claim: Al-Lihyani and others regard Quran as a verbal noun like ghufran, used for the thing recited by naming the object with its verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وعند اللحياني وجماعة هو مصدر كالغفران سمى به المقروء تسمية المفعول بالمصدر

rows.speaker: السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti chooses al-Shafi'i's account, which al-Alusi criticizes as unargued deference to the imam of his legal school.
rows.anchor: قال السيوطي : قلت والمختار عندي في هذه المسألة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi finds al-Zajjaj's analysis more convincing because hamza is the common form and six of the seven readers pronounce it; al-Zajjaj explains dropping the hamza but not retaining it, and al-Alusi begins to call Quran originally an adjective or verbal noun.
rows.anchor: قول الزجاج أرق من وجه إذ الشائع فيه الهمز وبه قرأ السبعة ما عدا إبن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The outward meaning must be mastered before seeking the inward: claiming esoteric understanding before mastering exoteric tafsir is like claiming to reach the room's front before entering through its door.
rows.anchor: وقالوا لا بد منه أولا إذ لا يطمع في الوصول إلى الباطن

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Quran has many subjects and layers, inexhaustible wonders, and outward recitation with inward interpretation; one who approaches it gently is saved, while one who approaches violently falls.
rows.anchor: عن إبن عباس قال : القرآن ذو شجون وفنون وظهور وبطون

rows.speaker: إبن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says that whoever seeks knowledge of the earliest and latest peoples should read the Quran; al-Alusi notes that this exceeds what outward exegesis alone provides.
rows.anchor: وقال إبن مسعود : من أراد علم الأولين والآخرين فليتل القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed trusted authority says each verse has sixty thousand understandings.
rows.anchor: وقد قال بعض من يوثق به لكل آية ستون ألف فهم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan transmits a Prophetic report that every verse has an outward and inward meaning, every letter a limit, and every limit an access point.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : لكل آية ظهر وبطن

rows.speaker: إبن النقيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Naqib defines the outward as meanings apparent to scholars of exoteric learning and the inward as secrets God discloses to people of spiritual realities.
rows.anchor: قال إبن النقيب أن ظاهرها ما ظهر من معانيها لأهل العلم بالظاهر وباطنها ما تضمنته

rows.speaker: إبن النقيب
rows.claim: For Ibn al-Naqib, a letter's limit marks the endpoint of its intended meaning, while its access point is a means of reaching enough knowledge of an obscure meaning or ruling.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله ولكل حرف حد أن لكل حرف منتهي فيما أراده الله تعالى من معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another transmitted wording says each verse has an outward, inward, limit, and access point.
rows.anchor: وقيل في رواية لكل آية ظهر وبطن وحد ومطلع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The outward is the wording and its conventional and signaled meanings used as routes to derive the five legal rulings.
rows.anchor: والمذكور بوساطة الألفاظ وتأليفاتها وضعا وإفادة وجعلها طرقا إلى إستنباط الأحكام الخمسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inward is the spirit of the words: divine speech apprehended beyond the faculties of ordinary discursive instruments through sanctified spiritual perception.
rows.anchor: وروح الألفاظ أعنى الكلام المعتلى عن المدارك الآلية بجواهر الروح القدسية هو البطن

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq's saying that God has manifested Himself to His servants in His Book, though they do not see, points to the access point as ascent from inward speech to the divine Speaker's Name.
rows.anchor: بقول الصادق لقد تجلى الله تعالى في كتابه لعباده ولكن لا يبصرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One mystical account places the limit between outward and inward or between inward and access point; the latter ascent recognizes the relation of attribute to Name and the servant's attribute's effacement under divine theophany.
rows.anchor: وإستهلاك صفة العبد تحت تجليات أنوار صفة المتكلم تعالى شأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view calls the outward tafsir, the inward ta'wil, the limit the reach of human understanding, and the access point the ascent from that reach to witnessing God.
rows.anchor: وقيل الظهر التفسير والبطن التأويل والحد ما تتناهى إليه الفهوم من معنى الكلام
